summary: An internal memo describing the datacomputer from a user's point of view. It was planned as a special ARPANET node devoted to managing a very large shared database, with a single data language used to describe and request data. The first service offering is described, along with how users reach it through access methods.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes a dedicated network computer for managing a large shared database. Programs describe the data they need, and the datacomputer can select records before sending them over the connection.

questions: how does the datacomputer organize records
why does the datacomputer select data subsets
subtitle: A user's view of a network service for shared data storage and retrieval.

tldr.problem: Programs using a large shared database may need only a small subset of its contents, and remote links can be narrow.
tldr.mechanism: The datacomputer stores described records, indexes data for selection, and exchanges record streams with programs using the network.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes DCAM-1 as the first service offering and explains the data language and operations from a user's perspective.

sections.title: The Datacomputer Service
sections.content:
The datacomputer is described as a specialized ARPA Network node dedicated to managing a large shared database. It presents itself to users as a black box with a data language that defines its operations, rather than as a general-purpose computing service.

The memo discusses the first service offering, DCAM-1 (Datacomputer Access Method-1), and says later access methods may generalize it. Programs on other computers retrieve and store the data.
sections.plainLanguage: The datacomputer is a network service devoted to data storage and management. Programs on other computers use its data language to request the service.

sections.title: Files, Records and Descriptions
sections.content:
Data is organized into named files, each with a file description that defines its structure. In the general model, a file contains uniquely numbered records, each containing named fields. Records can vary in format and size, and fields can vary in length.

The system can maintain indexes that point to records with selected properties. A unique, permanent record identifier lets an index or another record refer to a record. Data descriptions let the system parse records into named, typed elements and produce records from those elements.
sections.plainLanguage: A file contains records, and each record contains named fields. Descriptions tell the service how to interpret those fields, while indexes help locate records that match a request.

sections.title: Streams and Requests
sections.content:
Streams are sequences of records exchanged between using programs and the datacomputer. They follow the organization in a file description but cannot be indexed or stored permanently as streams; records pass one at a time.

The memo says most uses require selecting a subset before working with a file, especially for remote users. Indexes and logical operations such as AND, OR and NOT can help form subsets, after which records can be inspected and changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Records move through a stream one at a time, while files remain stored in the database. Selecting only relevant records can avoid sending an entire large file to a remote program.

sections.title: Maintenance and Example Uses
sections.content:
The basic file-maintenance operations are adding, deleting and replacing a field or record. The memo allows optional and variable-length fields and says file descriptions can be extended. When indexed fields change, the system can update related index entries if their rules are part of the description.

Possible applications listed include storing and retrieving large files, sequential file use, direct access, document retrieval, content-oriented retrieval, statistical analysis and modeling.
sections.plainLanguage: Users can add, remove or replace records and fields. The memo lists uses ranging from document search to statistical data analysis.
